subtitle: b. 1901, Surabaya, East Java (d. 1970) — 1st President of the Republic of Indonesia (1945–1967)
alt: If you still worship the sepia-toned myth of Bung Karno as a faultless revolutionary god, ask the starving peasants of 1965 how many three-hour anti-imperialist speeches it takes to fill an empty stomach when hyperinflation hits 635%. The man who liberated you from Dutch chains could not stomach a parliament that talked back to him, so on July 5, 1959 he strangled Indonesia's young constitutional democracy in its cradle, crowned himself President-for-Life like a feudal Javanese monarch, and threw anti-colonial heroes like Sutan Sjahrir and Mochtar Lubis into prison without trial. While ordinary families queued for rotting food, he burned the republic's last foreign reserves on vanity monuments in Jakarta and a reckless military confrontation in Borneo. Worse still, his arrogant Nasakom tightrope act, pitting a paranoid Army against millions of unarmed PKI peasants and workers, lit the fuse for the 1965–1966 slaughter; and when the rivers of Java and Bali ran red with the blood of the very followers who adored him, the Great Leader of the Revolution sat in his palace bargaining for his own titles until Suharto locked him away to die.
desc:
Born Kusno Sosrodihardjo in Surabaya, East Java, in 1901, Sukarno studied civil engineering at the Technische Hoogeschool te Bandoeng (now ITB) before founding the Indonesian National Party (PNI) in 1927 to spearhead the anti-colonial struggle against Dutch rule. Imprisoned at Sukamiskin and exiled to Ende and Bengkulu for over a decade, he articulated the five foundational principles of Pancasila in June 1945 and, alongside Mohammad Hatta, proclaimed Indonesia's independence on August 17, 1945—holding a war-torn archipelago together through sheer oratorical magnetism across four years of armed revolution.

Yet Sukarno despised the messy compromises of the 1950s parliamentary era. Following regional rebellions and deadlock in the Constituent Assembly, he joined forces with the Army high command on July 5, 1959 to dissolve parliament by decree, reinstate the executive-heavy 1945 Constitution, and inaugurate Guided Democracy (Demokrasi Terpimpin). Naming himself President-for-Life in 1963, he banned rival parties like Masyumi and PSI, silenced independent newspapers, and gambled the nation's survival on Nasakom—an increasingly volatile three-way balancing act between the Army, religious factions, and the three-million-strong Indonesian Communist Party (PKI) while the economy collapsed into 600% hyperinflation.

That cauldron exploded on the night of September 30, 1965, when the abortive G30S movement murdered six Army generals. Major General Suharto seized control of the military, unleashed the 1965–1966 anti-communist massacres that killed at least half a million Indonesians, and coerced Sukarno into signing the March 11, 1966 Supersemar order. Formally stripped of his presidential mandate by the Provisional MPR (MPRS) in March 1967 after its rejection of his Nawaksara accountability address, the founding father was kept isolated under military house arrest at Wisma Yaso in Jakarta until his death in June 1970.

subtitle: b. 1921, Kemusuk, Yogyakarta (d. 2008) — 2nd President of the Republic of Indonesia (1967–1998)
alt: If you'd think Indonesia would've gone anywhere under the so-called "ather of Development" except straight into the offshore bank accounts of Jalan Cendana, you are spitting on every unmarked mass grave dug between 1965 and 1998. For thirty-two years, that grandfatherly Javanese smile masked a cold-blooded kleptocrat who built his throne on half a million anti-communist corpses, gagged every dissident and newspaper with the Anti-Subversion Law, turned Aceh and East Timor into military slaughterhouses, and carved up the republic's forests, banks, and toll roads like birthday cake for his six insatiable children and their crony tycoons. When the rot finally caved in during the 1997–1998 crash, tens of millions of ordinary Indonesians were thrown into destitution and over a thousand burned alive inside Jakarta's shopping malls while Rp 144.5 trillion in BLBI liquidity vanished into conglomerate pockets. Yet the most sickening obscenity is what you allowed to happen afterward. The old tyrant never spent a single second behind bars, his youngest son served barely four years for paying hitmen to murder a Supreme Court justice, his Kopassus kidnappers were rewarded with general stars and ministry portfolios, and the nation he bled dry got back on its knees in November 2025 to crown its own butcher a National Hero.
desc:
Born in the village of Kemusuk, Yogyakarta, in 1921, Suharto rose through the Dutch colonial army (KNIL), the Japanese-sponsored PETA militia, and the revolutionary Indonesian Army, distinguishing himself in the March 1949 General Offensive in Yogyakarta. As commander of the Army Strategic Reserve (Kostrad) in October 1965, he crushed the September 30 Movement, extracted the March 11, 1966 Supersemar order from founding President Sukarno amid the 1965–1966 anti-communist purges, and ruled Indonesia for thirty-two years at the head of the military-backed New Order (Orde Baru). Backed by the Golkar electoral machine, the military's Dwifungsi doctrine, and US-trained technocrats, his regime delivered decades of industrial growth and rice self-sufficiency while ruthlessly crushing labor unions, press freedom, and political dissent.

From his family residence at No. 8 Jalan Cendana in Menteng, Suharto, his six children—led by Tutut (Siti Hardiyanti Rukmana, b. 1949), Bambang Trihatmodjo (b. 1953), Titiek (Siti Hediati Hariyadi, b. 1959), and Tommy (Hutomo Mandala Putra, b. 1962)—and seven tax-exempt presidential foundations (including Supersemar and Dakab) amassed an estimated $15 billion to $35 billion fortune through state monopolies in toll roads, cloves, oil trading, television, and the Timor national car. Forced to resign on May 21, 1998 after the Asian Financial Crisis and the May riots shattered his regime, Suharto retreated to Jalan Cendana under military protection. Although the November 1998 MPR Special Session explicitly named Suharto in TAP MPR No. XI/MPR/1998 as a target of anti-corruption investigations, Habibie's government issued an SP3 halting the probe in October 1999.

When President Gus Dur reopened the prosecution in 2000, Suharto's doctors testified that a series of strokes had left him permanently unfit to stand trial, and in May 2006 the Attorney General's Office issued an SKP3 permanently dropping all criminal charges. Youngest son Tommy Suharto was convicted of a Rp 95 billion Bulog land-swap fraud in 2000, went underground, and paid hitmen to assassinate Supreme Court Justice Syafiuddin Kartasasmita in July 2001; sentenced to 15 years in 2002, he had his term cut to 10 years by the Supreme Court and walked free on parole in October 2006 after serving barely four years. Suharto died in January 2008 at age 86 with a full military state funeral, his name was formally scrubbed from TAP MPR No. XI/MPR/1998 in September 2024, and on November 10, 2025, his former son-in-law President Prabowo Subianto officially proclaimed him a National Hero (Pahlawan Nasional).

subtitle: b. 1936, Parepare, South Sulawesi (d. 2019) | 3rd President of the Republic of Indonesia (1998–1999)
alt: Before you weep over movies painting B.J. Habibie as a misunderstood romantic genius and the sainted father of Indonesian democracy, ask yourself where his conscience was for the twenty-four years he spent feasting at Suharto's table. Calling the dictator his 'spiritual father' and praising him as Super Genius Suharto, Habibie happily raided Rp 400 billion from the Reforestation Fund to subsidize his pet IPTN aircraft factories while Indonesian villages lacked clean water, and built ICMI to give an aging autocracy an Islamic fig leaf. Even when history dumped the presidency into his lap in May 1998, every democratic reform he signed was wrung out of him by the threat of the students in the streets and a gun held to the treasury's head by the IMF. Behind closed doors, he was still Suharto's loyal apprentice, caught red-handed on a tapped phone line with Attorney General Andi Ghalib staging a fake, deferential corruption inquiry into Cendana, letting his palace Tim Sukses loot Rp 546 billion from Bank Bali to buy MPR delegates, and casually tossing East Timor a referendum without lifting a finger to stop General Wiranto's militias from burning Dili to the ground.
desc:
Born in Parepare, South Sulawesi, in 1936, Bacharuddin Jusuf Habibie lost his father at fourteen and won a scholarship to study aeronautical engineering at RWTH Aachen in West Germany, earning his doctorate summa cum laude in 1965 and rising to become a vice president at Messerschmitt-Bölkow-Blohm. Summoned home by Suharto in 1974 to spearhead Indonesia's high-tech industrial drive, he served for twenty years as Minister of Research and Technology (1978–1998), pouring billions of state dollars into the IPTN aircraft complex in Bandung and chairing the Association of Indonesian Muslim Intellectuals (ICMI). Elevated from the Vice Presidency on May 21, 1998 upon Suharto's resignation, Suharto's lifelong protégé inherited a bankrupt treasury, a collapsed rupiah, and a republic on the edge of violent fracture.

Over seventeen frantic months in office, the frenetic technocrat presided over the most rapid democratic opening in Indonesian history. Desperate to win domestic legitimacy and unlock IMF bailout tranches, he freed political prisoners, abolished SIUPP press censorship, legalized independent labor unions and dozens of political parties, emancipated Bank Indonesia, enacted sweeping Regional Autonomy, organized the June 7, 1999 multiparty election, and offered East Timor its August 1999 self-determination ballot. Yet his refusal to prosecute Suharto, exposed in a leaked February 1999 wiretap with Attorney General Andi Ghalib and sealed by an October 1999 SP3 termination order—combined with the Rp 546 billion Bank Bali ('Baligate') campaign slush-fund scandal and military fury over the loss of East Timor, proved fatal to his political survival.

On the night of October 19–20, 1999, after dozens of Golkar delegates loyal to party chairman Akbar Tandjung defected behind the secret-ballot curtain, the MPR rejected Habibie's Accountability Speech by a vote of 355 to 322, forcing him to withdraw his presidential candidacy before dawn. In retirement, he divided his time between Germany and Jakarta, founded the Habibie Center, and watched his public memory soften into that of an accidental democratic reformer before his death in September 2019 and burial at Kalibata Heroes Cemetery beside his wife, Hasri Ainun Besari.

subtitle: b. 1940, Jombang, East Java (d. 2009) — Founder of PKB & 4th President of the Republic of Indonesia (1999–2001)
alt: Strip away the untouchable halo of the saintly pluralist and look closely at how Gus Dur actually climbed into the presidential palace, and how recklessly he squandered the mandate of Reformasi once he got there. In 1998 and 1999, while students were still bleeding on the asphalt of Semanggi, this supposed moral conscience of the nation was busy paying friendly visits to Suharto at Jalan Cendana, hugging Megawati in public while sharpening knives behind her back with Amien Rais's sectarian Central Axis, and riding the votes of Golkar and ABRI into office by letting clerics declare a woman unfit to lead. Once inside Istana Merdeka, he treated the republic like his private pesantren, announcing he would pardon Suharto if he ever went to trial, mocking the elected parliament as a 'kindergarten,' firing cabinet ministers almost every month, and shrugging while his personal masseur walked off with Rp 35 billion from Bulog alongside an undocumented $2 million gift from the Sultan of Brunei. And when his own coalition finally turned on him in July 2001, the great democrat tried to save his throne like a tinpot autocrat, ordering the military to dissolve parliament by midnight decree and handing the keys of the state straight back to the New Order sharks.
desc:
Born in Jombang, East Java, in 1940 into the revered clerical dynasty that founded Nahdlatul Ulama (NU), Abdurrahman Wahid—universally known as Gus Dur—was educated at traditional Javanese pesantren before studying in Cairo and Baghdad. Elected Chairman of NU in 1984, he led Indonesia's 40-million-strong traditionalist Muslim movement for fifteen years, championing religious pluralism, defending ethnic Chinese and Christian minorities, and infuriating both New Order hardliners and modernist ICMI rivals.

Despite suffering a near-fatal stroke in early 1998 that left him legally blind, Gus Dur founded the National Awakening Party (PKB) in July 1998, capturing 51 seats in the 1999 MPR. Throughout the transition, he bewildered allies and enemies alike with his erratic, Machiavellian maneuvers—visiting Suharto at Jalan Cendana to keep old-guard channels open, hosting the reformist Ciganjur Summit in November 1998, and publicly embracing Megawati Sukarnoputri while quietly allowing Amien Rais's Central Axis (Poros Tengah) to float his name as an Islamic compromise candidate. Following the rejection of Habibie's Accountability Speech on October 20, 1999, Gus Dur rode a backroom coalition of Islamic parties, Akbar Tandjung's Golkar, and ABRI to defeat Megawati 373 to 313 and become Indonesia's fourth President.

In office, Gus Dur boldly abolished the Ministry of Information, repealed the thirty-year ban on Chinese cultural celebrations (Keppres No. 6/2000), apologized for the 1965–1966 anti-communist killings, allowed the Morning Star flag to fly in Papua, and forced General Wiranto out of his cabinet. Yet his chaotic administrative style, relentless cabinet sackings, and bitter clashes with the DPR over the Buloggate and Bruneigate financial scandals alienated the very coalition that installed him. Impeached by an MPR Special Session on July 23, 2001 hours after issuing a failed midnight decree (Maklumat) to dissolve parliament and freeze Golkar, he stepped down peacefully and remained an iconic voice for minority rights until his death in December 2009, receiving the title of National Hero in November 2025.

subtitle: b. 1947, Yogyakarta — Chairwoman of PDI-P & 5th President of the Republic of Indonesia (2001–2004)
alt: Ask the pedicab drivers, street vendors, and student activists who had their skulls cracked open by military truncheons on July 27, 1996 (Kudatuli) what they actually got when Megawati Sukarnoputri finally ascended to her father's throne. Nothing. Nothing except the stony silence of a dynastic matriarch who believed her last name entitled her to the republic without lifting a finger for the wong cilik who bled for her. Too arrogant to lower herself to parliamentary horse-trading in October 1999, she let Amien Rais and Akbar Tandjung steal the presidency right out from under her 33.7% plurality. And when she finally inherited the palace in 2001, the former icon of resistance governed like a conservative New Order regent, signing the infamous Release and Discharge (SKL) immunity letters via Inpres No. 8/2002 so Suharto's richest BLBI banking parasites could walk away with tens of trillions of stolen taxpayer rupiah, placing Aceh under full martial law, and rehabilitating the very generals who raided her own party headquarters in 1996, before spending the next twenty years running PDI-P like a feudal court where elected presidents are treated as mere 'party officers' (petugas partai).
desc:
Born in Yogyakarta in 1947 during the Indonesian National Revolution as the eldest daughter of founding President Sukarno and Fatmawati, Megawati Sukarnoputri spent her early adulthood outside politics after her father was deposed by Suharto in 1966. Drawn into parliament in 1987 by the Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI), she was elected PDI Chairwoman in 1993 in open defiance of the New Order's intelligence apparatus. Threatened by her immense grassroots appeal among the urban and rural poor (wong cilik), the Suharto regime engineered a rival congress in Medan to oust her and backed the bloody July 27, 1996 raid on her party headquarters (Peristiwa Kudatuli), turning her silent endurance into the premier symbol of civilian resistance.

After Suharto's fall, she reorganized her movement as the Indonesian Democratic Party of Struggle (PDI-P) and swept the June 7, 1999 legislative election with 33.7% of the national vote and 153 seats in the MPR. Convinced that her electoral plurality entitled her to the presidency by birthright, Megawati remained aloof from the frantic coalition-building in Senayan, refusing to court Islamic parties or regional caucuses. During the October 1999 General Session, her caucus voted overwhelmingly to reject Habibie's Accountability Speech, only to be outmaneuvered days later when Amien Rais's Central Axis and Akbar Tandjung's Golkar bloc united behind Abdurrahman Wahid (Gus Dur), defeating her 373 to 313 and leaving her to accept the Vice Presidency to calm her rioting supporters across Java and Bali.

When the MPR impeached and removed Gus Dur in July 2001, Megawati ascended to become Indonesia's fifth President (2001–2004), presiding over macroeconomic stabilization, constitutional amendments introducing direct presidential elections, the establishment of the KPK, a renewed military offensive under martial law in Aceh, and the controversial issuance of Release and Discharge certificates (SKL) granting legal immunity to major BLBI bank debtors. Despite losing the 2004 and 2009 presidential elections to her former security minister Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono, she remains the undisputed matriarch of Indonesian party politics as lifelong Chairwoman of PDI-P and Chair of the Steering Committee of the Pancasila Ideology Development Agency (BPIP).

subtitle: b. 1949, Pacitan, East Java — ABRI Chief of Sociopolitical Affairs (1998–1999) & 6th President of the Republic of Indonesia (2004–2014)
alt: Look back at the ten-year anesthesia of Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono's presidency and ask yourself what a polished voice, melancholy pop albums, and choreographed press conferences actually bought this country besides a decade of cowardly paralysis. In 1998, as the smooth-talking architect of ABRI's 'New Paradigm' (Paradigma Baru), SBY ran the ultimate institutional con job. Trading away a handful of parliamentary seats so the Army could preserve its lucrative territorial command network (Kodam) and shield every single general from human rights tribunals. Elected in two landslides by playing the wounded victim, he spent ten years in the palace paralyzed by his obsession with his own approval ratings. Under his watch, the intelligence masterminds who poisoned human rights lawyer Munir Said Thalib on a Garuda flight walked free while the presidential fact-finding report conveniently 'disappeared,' hardline vigilantes torched Ahmadiyah and Christian churches while his police stood watching, the state bled Rp 6.7 trillion in the murky Bank Century bailout, and SBY went on television to sigh "Saya prihatin" ('I am concerned') while the top leadership of his own Democratic Party looted the treasury blind in the Hambalang corruption scandal.
desc:
Born in Pacitan, East Java, in 1949, Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono graduated at the top of his Military Academy class in 1973 and married Kristiani Herrawati ('Ani'), daughter of feared RPKAD commando commander Sarwo Edhie Wibowo who led the 1965–1966 purges. Educated at US military staff colleges, Yudhoyono became the public face of the Army's intellectual reform wing in 1998–1999 while serving as ABRI Chief of Sociopolitical Affairs (Kassospol) and later Chief of Territorial Affairs (Kaster) under General Wiranto.

Sitting on the August 1998 Officers' Honor Council (DKP) that administratively discharged Prabowo Subianto, Yudhoyono served as the chief architect of ABRI's Paradigma Baru ('New Paradigm'). Recognizing that public fury after Suharto's fall threatened the military's institutional survival, he engineered a calculated tactical retreat: severing ABRI's formal ties with Golkar, separating the National Police (Polri) from the military command structure in April 1999, and accepting a phased reduction of unelected legislative seats in exchange for preserving the Army's village-level territorial command network (Kodam) and insulating the officer corps from human rights courts.

Entering civilian government in October 1999, Yudhoyono served as Minister of Mines and Energy and later Coordinating Minister for Political and Security Affairs under both Gus Dur and Megawati. After skilfully turning a public falling-out with Megawati's inner circle into grassroots sympathy in early 2004, he ran on the ticket of his newly founded Democratic Party and won Indonesia's first direct presidential election in a landslide. Serving two full terms (2004–2014), he oversaw the landmark 2005 Helsinki Peace Accord ending the thirty-year insurgency in Aceh and rode the 2000s global commodity boom, before his second term was battered by chronic policy hesitation, the Bank Century bailout inquiry, and the Hambalang graft convictions that decimated his party's top leadership.

subtitle: b. 1961, Surakarta, Central Java — 7th President of the Republic of Indonesia (2014–2024)
alt: Ask yourself how it felt to march, donate, and weep in 2014 for the humble carpenter's son in the rolled-up white sleeves only to watch Joko Widodo methodically strangle every single Reformasi institution that made his rise possible. You elected him, we elected him, as the antidote to the oligarchs and the New Order generals; instead, he packed his cabinet with both, bought off the entire parliament into a bloated super-coalition that erased opposition oversight, and in September 2019 gutted the Corruption Eradication Commission (KPK) while students were beaten and tear-gassed in the streets. Behind the folksy blusukan smile and endless ribbons cut on toll roads and the debt-soaked Nusantara (IKN) vanity capital in the Kalimantan jungle, Jokowi hollowed out Indonesian democracy from the inside. In October 2023, when two terms were not enough for his bloodline, he let his own brother-in-law, Chief Justice Anwar Usman, rig the Constitutional Court's age rules so his thirty-six-year-old son Gibran could ride into the Vice Presidency on the ticket of Prabowo Subianto: betraying the party that made him and handing the republic straight back to the ghosts of 1998.
desc:
Born in Surakarta (Solo), Central Java, in 1961 as the son of a small-scale timber seller, Joko Widodo—popularly known as Jokowi—studied forestry at Gadjah Mada University in Yogyakarta before building a furniture export business in his hometown. Completely outside Jakarta's military, bureaucratic, and party oligarchies during the 1998–1999 transition, his political ascent was the ultimate product of the post-1999 Regional Autonomy (Otonomi Daerah) and direct local election (Pilkada) reforms initiated after Suharto's fall.

Elected Mayor of Surakarta in 2005 on the PDI-P ticket, Jokowi won national acclaim for his unannounced neighborhood inspections (blusukan), bureaucratic cleanups, and peaceful relocation of street vendors. Propelled by Megawati Sukarnoputri's party into the Jakarta governorship in 2012, he defeated former general Prabowo Subianto in the bitterly polarized 2014 and 2019 presidential elections to become the first Indonesian President without roots in the New Order political or military elite.

Over two terms in office (2014–2024), Jokowi spearheaded a massive infrastructure drive across the archipelago, banned raw mineral exports to force domestic nickel smelting, and launched the multibillion-dollar Nusantara (IKN) capital city project in East Kalimantan. At the same time, he absorbed former rivals—including Prabowo and Golkar—into a dominant executive coalition, signed the 2019 KPK Law revision that crippled Indonesia's anti-graft commission, and pushed through the controversial Omnibus Job Creation Law. In late 2023, breaking openly with Megawati and PDI-P, he threw his state patronage network behind his two-time rival Prabowo Subianto after the Constitutional Court—chaired by Jokowi's brother-in-law Anwar Usman—carved out an age exception allowing Jokowi's eldest son, Gibran Rakabuming Raka, to run and win as Prabowo's Vice President in February 2024.

subtitle: b. 1951, Jakarta — Commander of Kopassus (1995–1998) & Kostrad (1998); 8th President of the Republic of Indonesia (2024–present)
alt: Tell the mothers in black who have stood in the rain outside Merdeka Palace every single Thursday for nearly twenty-eight years (Aksi Kamisan) that a cartoon avatar and a clumsy gemoy TikTok dance were all it took for you to erase the thirteen student and labor activists who never came home from Kopassus cells in 1998. You watched the man who married into Jalan Cendana, commanded the red berets whose Tim Mawar kidnappers electrocuted pro-democracy students at Cijantung, and was stripped of his Kostrad command on May 22, 1998 after deploying armed troops around Habibie's residence, walk right through the front gates of the presidency without ever facing a court-martial. And what did he do once you handed him the republic in 2024? He appointed convicted Tim Mawar abductors to run your customs service, your cyber intelligence agency, and your provinces; pushed active-duty TNI officers back into civilian bureaucracy; and stood inside Istana Negara on November 10, 2025 to pin the medal of National Hero onto the corpse of his former father-in-law Suharto—proving once and for all that the New Order never died in May 1998, it just waited for you to forget.
desc:
Born in Jakarta in 1951 as the son of prominent economist and former cabinet minister Sumitro Djojohadikusumo, Prabowo Subianto spent much of his youth in exile in Europe and Malaysia before graduating from the Indonesian Military Academy in 1974. Marrying Suharto's daughter Siti Hediati Hariyadi ('Titiek') in 1983, he built a fierce reputation as a counter-insurgency field officer in East Timor and rose rapidly under his father-in-law's patronage to command the elite special forces (Kopassus, 1995–1998) and the 35,000-troop Army Strategic Reserve (Kostrad) in March 1998.

In the final months of the New Order, Kopassus Group IV's covert Tim Mawar ('Rose Team') squad abducted and tortured more than twenty pro-democracy activists—nine of whom emerged alive from secret cells, while thirteen remained permanently disappeared. During the May 13–15, 1998 Jakarta riots, the government's Joint Fact-Finding Team (TGPF) urged an investigation into Prabowo's attendance at a controversial May 14 meeting at Kostrad headquarters while the capital burned. On May 22, 1998, twenty-four hours after Habibie was sworn in, Habibie and General Wiranto stripped Prabowo of his Kostrad command after armed troops deployed around the presidential palace and Habibie's Kuningan residence. In August 1998, an internal Officers' Honor Council (DKP) administratively discharged Prabowo from military service over the activist abductions, but he was never brought before a court-martial and spent several years in self-imposed exile in Jordan.

Returning to Indonesia, Prabowo founded the Gerindra Party in 2008 and ran unsuccessfully for Vice President in 2009 and President in 2014 and 2019. Although Komnas HAM's 2006 investigative dossier on the 1997–1998 disappearances and a 2009 DPR recommendation for an Ad Hoc Human Rights Court remained permanently stalled at the Attorney General's Office, Prabowo was rehabilitated by his former rival Joko Widodo as Minister of Defense in 2019, awarded an honorary four-star General rank in early 2024, and—running alongside Jokowi's son Gibran while rebranded on social media as an endearing grandfather (gemoy)—won the February 2024 presidential election in a 58.6% landslide to become the eighth President of Indonesia, proclaiming Suharto a National Hero in November 2025.
